overview.text: The Acropolis of Athens is a steep-sided rocky hill rising above the city and crowned by ancient monuments. Fortified as early as the Mycenaean period, it gradually became a sanctuary associated especially with Athena, patron goddess of Athens. Its best-known buildings—the Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaia, and Temple of Athena Nike—were largely created in a fifth-century BCE building program under Pericles. Their architecture and sculpture make the site an important record of ancient Greek religion and art, and influenced later architecture. The Parthenon was badly damaged in 1687, when stored gunpowder exploded.

key_facts.text: The rocky summit is steep on all sides except the west, and fortification walls have surrounded it for more than 3,300 years.
The first fortification wall dates to the 13th century BCE and enclosed a Mycenaean ruler’s residence.
The Acropolis gradually took on a religious character from the 8th century BCE, with the establishment of Athena’s cult.

The fifth-century BCE building program included the Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaia, and Temple of Athena Nike; UNESCO notes that the monuments later influenced Neoclassical architecture around the world.
In 1687, an explosion of gunpowder stored inside the Parthenon damaged the building and scattered architectural pieces around the hill.
